messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 19
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Fast Food Worker
- Trauma Type: Natural disaster
- Pcl5: 40

**Vignette: Marcus**

Marcus is nineteen years old and works the morning shift at a burger chain about two miles from the apartment he shares with his older cousin. He is quiet when he first arrives for sessions, pulling at the strings of his hoodie and glancing toward the window more than he looks at the therapist. He seems older than his age in some ways — careful, measured — and much younger in others.

Eighteen months ago, Marcus was living with his mother and younger sister in a small house in a river town in the American Midwest when a flash flood tore through their neighborhood in the early hours of a Tuesday morning. He remembers waking to his mother screaming his name. The water was already at his knees by the time he reached the hallway. He grabbed his sister, who was seven at the time, and the three of them climbed onto the roof through the attic hatch. They stayed there for four hours in the dark, the water rising to the eaves below them, his sister shaking against his chest, his mother praying quietly beside him. He did not pray. He watched the black water and listened to what he describes as the sound of the neighborhood disappearing — fences giving way, cars shifting, things he couldn't name moving through the dark.

They survived. Their house did not. They lost almost everything, and within a few weeks Marcus's mother moved with his sister to stay with family in another state. Marcus, who had just turned eighteen and felt he shouldn't uproot his mother's plans, stayed behind and moved in with his cousin. He got the fast food job quickly, needing income, and tells himself he is fine because he goes to work and pays his share of the rent.

But mornings are hard. He wakes between three and four a.m. most nights, heart already pounding, convinced the floor is wet. He lies still in the dark and listens for water. He knows it isn't rational, but knowing doesn't stop it. By the time he gets up for his shift, he is already exhausted, running on two or three hours of sleep and a large coffee he drinks in the parking lot before clocking in.

At work, the sound of the floor drain gurgling in the kitchen sends a jolt through him that he can't explain to his coworkers. He has learned to position himself away from it. On rainy days, he checks his phone compulsively for weather alerts, even when the sky is only overcast. He has called in sick on days when the forecast showed heavy rain, not because he planned to but because he simply could not make himself leave the apartment. His manager has noticed. Marcus tells him he's been having headaches.

He doesn't talk about the flood with his coworkers or his cousin. When his cousin asks how he's sleeping, Marcus says fine. He has texted his mother every day since the flood — sometimes three or four times — needing to know she and his sister are okay, though he struggles to explain why the need feels so urgent even on ordinary days.

What troubles Marcus most, he says, is that he doesn't feel like himself anymore. He used to play pickup basketball on weekends and had a group of friends from high school he'd see regularly. Now he declines invitations, not because he doesn't want to go but because being around groups of people in spaces he can't control makes him edgy and worn out in a way he can't articulate. He sits in his room instead, watching videos on his phone until his eyes give out.

He describes the night of the flood matter-of-factly, with few visible emotions, until he mentions holding his sister on the roof. Then he stops talking and looks at the window for a long moment. He says he keeps thinking about what would have happened if he hadn't woken up. He says he doesn't know why he can't just move on.
